claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991 and Guo et al., 2014.

claims.claim: According to the amplifier hypothesis, MYC-amplifier-gain increases as the level of signaling to a transcriptionally activated promoter increases.
claims.source: According to this explanation, MYC-amplifier-gain increases as the level of signaling to a transcriptionally activated promoter increases.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the amplifier hypothesis being tested in the study.

claims.claim: Highly expressed genes are disproportionately amplified compared with less expressed genes according to the amplifier model.
claims.source: Thus, highly expressed genes are disproportionately amplified compared with less expressed genes.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction of the amplifier hypothesis being tested.

claims.claim: Both the global amplifier and gene selective activator models for MYC action have been buttressed by large-scale genome-wide expression and ChIP-Seq studies.
claims.source: Both the global amplifier and gene selective activator models for MYC action have been buttressed by large-scale genome-wide expression and ChIP-Seq studies—sometimes sustaining opposite conclusions from the same data (Kress et al., 2015; Lorenzin et al., 2016; Sabò et al., 2014; Tesi et al., 2019; Wolf et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to genomic studies.

claims.claim: The selection of statistical parameters and models, as well as the choice of computational algorithms, determines the outputs of '-omics' studies.
claims.source: Because the selection of statistical parameters and models, as well as the choice of computational algorithms, determines their outputs, these '-omics' studies have failed to resolve the essential role of MYC in transcription.
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of the limitations of omics studies stated in the introduction.

claims.claim: MYC interacts with a wide assortment of transcription and chromatin components as well as with other proteins both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: MYC interacts with a wide assortment of transcription and chromatin components as well as with other proteins both in vitro and in vivo (Agrawal et al., 2010; Baluapuri et al., 2019; Büchel et al., 2017; Chakravorty et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2014; Dingar et al., 2015; Kalkat et al., 2018; Koch et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies of MYC protein interactions.

claims.claim: Total RNA increased to near statistical significance at 6 hr and became statistically significant after 10 and 14 hr following tamoxifen treatment of HO15.19 MYC-ER cells.
claims.source: From an already large baseline, total RNA increased to near statistical significance at 6 hr and became so, after 10 and 14 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The output of MYC protein was linearly related to the transfected amount of the MYC-encoding plasmid.
claims.source: Immunoblot of transfected cells confirmed that the output of MYC protein was linearly related to the transfected amount of the MYC-encoding plasmid (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Upon treatment with DEX and MYC, GREtkLuc increased ~15 fold, whereas the other reporters remained unresponsive.
claims.source: Upon treatment with DEX and MYC, GREtkLuc increased ~15 fold, whereas the other reporters remained unresponsive.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the reporter assays described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Upon activation by GR and DEX, GREtkLuc became more MYC-responsive just as predicted by the amplifier theory.
claims.source: Therefore, upon activation by GR and DEX, GREtkLuc became more MYC-responsive just as predicted by the amplifier theory (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 1C in the context of the amplifier hypothesis.

claims.claim: As the level of transfected MYC-EGFP was progressively increased, the reporter response increased non-linearly as if MYC activation enhanced the efficiency of further MYC activation.
claims.source: As the level of transfected MYC-EGFP was progressively increased, the reporter response increased non-linearly as if MYC activation enhanced the efficiency of further MYC activation (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: 10058-F4 dramatically impaired amplification of GR/DEX-driven GREtkLuc expression by MYC.
claims.source: This well-characterized inhibitor of MYC-MAX dimerization (Wang et al., 2007) not only dramatically impaired amplification, but unexpectedly almost abolished the DEX-dependent activation of GREtkLuc by GR in U2OS cells that express only endogenous MYC (Figure 1C vs. D, red bracket).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Figure 1C and 1D, with citation to Wang et al., 2007 for the characterization of F4.

claims.claim: 10058-F4 almost abolished the DEX-dependent activation of GREtkLuc by GR in U2OS cells that express only endogenous MYC.
claims.source: This well-characterized inhibitor of MYC-MAX dimerization (Wang et al., 2007) not only dramatically impaired amplification, but unexpectedly almost abolished the DEX-dependent activation of GREtkLuc by GR in U2OS cells that express only endogenous MYC (Figure 1C vs. D, red bracket).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing Figure 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: The activation of the GREtk-promoter by Dex in U2OS cells is dependent on MYC-Max dimers, whether endogenous or transfected.
claims.source: This result indicates that the activation of the GREtk-promoter by Dex in U2OS cells is dependent on MYC-Max dimers, whether endogenous or transfected.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the F4 inhibition data from Figure 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: The affinity of MYC-MAX for the best binding of all possible eight-mer base sequences exceed those of the worst by less than 100-fold.
claims.source: The affinity of MYC-MAX for the best binding of all possible eight-mer base sequences exceed those of the worst by less than 100-fold (modest for sequence specific recognition) (Guo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claims.claim: One perfect E-box has the same DNA binding avidity as 100 bp of non-E-box DNA.
claims.source: So, one perfect E-box has the same DNA binding avidity as 100 bp of non-E-box DNA, and the insertion of a perfect E-box into 200 bp of E-box-less promoter DNA would then be expected to increase the region's net avidity for MYC by ≈1.5 fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on the binding affinity data, illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Addition of Dex licensed 1.5x greater MYC amplification of GRE-E-box-tkLuc than of GREtkLuc by exogenous MYC, exactly as predicted.
claims.source: Addition of Dex licensed 1.5x greater MYC amplification of GRE-E-box-tkLuc than of GREtkLuc by exogenous MYC, exactly as predicted (Figure 2B vs. C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: At low levels of intracellular MYC, MAX-MAX dimers prevail and may bind to E-boxes more specifically, but less avidly than the more sparse MYC-MAX.
claims.source: At low levels of intracellular MYC, MAX-MAX dimers prevail and may bind to E-boxes more specifically, but less avidly than the more sparse MYC-MAX (Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014 and Guo et al., 2014.

claims.claim: MAX-MAX dimers possess intrinsic repressor activity.
claims.source: MAX-MAX dimers possess intrinsic repressor activity (Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014), and MAX heterodimerizes with other repressive bHLH-ZIP proteins (Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Substitutions within MBII considerably attenuated amplifier gain.
claims.source: Although mutation of no individual MB abrogated amplification compared with wild-type MYC (Figure 3B–F), substitutions within MBII considerably attenuated amplifier gain (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: At high levels of transfected MYC, substitution mutations within MBIII dramatically boosted the amplifier gain on GR activated reporter expression.
claims.source: Strikingly, at high levels of transfected MYC, substitution mutations within MBIII dramatically boosted the amplifier gain on GR activated reporter expression (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: MBIV substitutions also increased MYC amplification.
claims.source: MBIV substitutions also increased MYC amplification (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Over-amplification by the mutant MBs III and IV was attenuated by co-mutation of MBI.
claims.source: Over-amplification by the mutant MBs III and IV was attenuated by co-mutation of MBI (Figure 3G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claims.claim: Mutant MBIII-hyperactivation does not result from increased levels of expressed protein.
claims.source: Mutant MBIII-hyperactivation does not result from increased levels of expressed protein. In fact, MBIII-mutant protein levels were markedly reduced compared to wild-type MYC (Figure 3I; it should be noted that the rabbit monoclonal antibody used to detect MYC binds with epitopes far-removed to the amino-terminal-side of MBIII and IV and that immunoblots of wild-type and mutant MYC-EGFP fusion proteins using either anti-MYC or anti-EGFP are equivalent, vide infra).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: A striking inverse relationship was apparent between activity and MYC levels with the highly active MBIII and MBIV mutants sustaining the least amount of MYC, whereas minimally active double and triple MB-mutants displayed the highest levels of MYC protein.
claims.source: A striking inverse relationship was apparent between activity and MYC levels with the highly active MBIII and MBIV mutants sustaining the least amount of MYC, whereas minimally active double and triple MB-mutants displayed the highest levels of MYC protein.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data plotted in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: The inverse relationship between abundance and activity is consistent with a previous suggestion that transactivation by MYC and its turnover are coupled.
claims.source: This inverse relationship between abundance and activity is consistent with a previous suggestion that transactivation by MYC and its turnover are coupled (Farrell et al., 2013; Farrell and Sears, 2014; Kim et al., 2003; Molinari et al., 1999; Salghetti et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to multiple studies on MYC turnover.

claims.claim: The transfected MYC increased reporter RNA levels.
claims.source: The transfected MYC increased reporter RNA levels.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from the RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: MYC mutations do not discriminate activation of expression genes with or without E-boxes.
claims.source: Thus, MYC mutations do not discriminate activation of expression genes with or without E-boxes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 4 comparing E-box and non-E-box reporters.

claims.claim: Co-transfected MYC progressively amplified GAL4/VP16-driven reporter activity.
claims.source: Co-transfected MYC progressively amplified GAL4/VP16-driven reporter activity (Figure 5C), just as it had for GR.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The output of Gal4/VP16 and MYC together exceeded those of either transactivator alone, indicating non-redundant mechanisms.
claims.source: The output of Gal4/VP16 and MYC together exceeded those of either transactivator alone, indicating non-redundant mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from Figure 5C showing synergistic effects.

claims.claim: Mutation of MBIII dramatically raised the gain on amplification of GAL4/VP16 at high levels of MYC.
claims.source: Similar to GR and PR, mutation of MBIII dramatically raised the gain on amplification of GAL4/VP16 at high levels of MYC (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: MBIII helps to limit positive feedback of MYC on VP16-driven expression.
claims.source: This result suggests that MBIII helps to limit positive feedback of MYC on VP16-driven expression.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MBIII mutation data from Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Co-mutation of MBI and MBIII reduced the excessive gain of the MBIII mutation back to wild-type levels.
claims.source: Likewise, co-mutation of MBI and MBIII reduced the excessive gain of the MBIII mutation back to wild-type levels (Figure 5E), inviting consideration of MBI as a regulator of mutant MBIII activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Alone, endogenous levels of U2OS MYC sustained only low basal mCherry expression from the E-box-less minimal GAL4UAS promoter.
claims.source: Alone, endogenous levels of U2OS MYC sustained only low basal mCherry expression from the E-box-less minimal GAL4UAS promoter (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Induction of MYC with added Dox or separately transfecting GAL4/VP16, each failed to augment reporter output.
claims.source: Induction of MYC with added Dox or separately transfecting GAL4/VP16, each failed to augment reporter output (upper right and lower left panels of Figure 6B); however together, transfected GAL4/VP16 and induced-MYC cooperated to raise chromosomal report output (lower right panel of Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Transfected GAL4/VP16 and induced-MYC cooperated to raise chromosomal reporter output.
claims.source: Induction of MYC with added Dox or separately transfecting GAL4/VP16, each failed to augment reporter output (upper right and lower left panels of Figure 6B); however together, transfected GAL4/VP16 and induced-MYC cooperated to raise chromosomal report output (lower right panel of Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Upon MYC induction with Dox, E-box-bearing reporter output intensified and achieved its highest levels when GAL4/VP16 was co-transfected.
claims.source: Upon MYC induction with Dox, E-box-bearing reporter output intensified and achieved its highest levels when GAL4/VP16 was co-transfected (lower right panel of Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: MYC binds at both E-box-less and E-box-bearing promoters, but a bit more efficiently at the latter in accord with the amplifier hypothesis.
claims.source: These data anticipate that MYC binds at both E-box-less and E-box-bearing promoters (Guo et al., 2014; Nie et al., 2012), but a bit more efficiently at the latter in accord with the amplifier hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from Figure 6 with support from citations to Guo et al., 2014 and Nie et al., 2012.

claims.claim: MYC-amplification to mid-level expression was resilient to mutation of individual MYC boxes.
claims.source: As with transient transfection, MYC-amplification to mid-level expression was resilient to mutation of individual MYC boxes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the lentivirus experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Without Gal4/VP16, and without doxycycline treatment, uninduced MYC-EGFP binding at the integrated E-box-less promoter did not rise above the background.
claims.source: Without Gal4/VP16, and without doxycycline treatment, uninduced MYC-EGFP binding at the integrated E-box-less promoter did not rise above the background (Figure 7A, lanes 1 vs. 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Inclusion of an E-box licensed low levels of MYC-EGFP binding.
claims.source: Inclusion of an E-box licensed low levels of MYC-EGFP binding (Figure 7A, lanes 5 vs. 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Without GAL4/VP16, induction with Dox modestly augmented MYC-EGFP recruitment to the reporter-promoter both in the absence and presence of an E-box.
claims.source: Also, without GAL4/VP16, induction with Dox modestly augmented MYC-EGFP recruitment to the reporter-promoter both in the absence and presence of an E-box (Figure 7A, lanes 3 vs. 4, 7 vs. 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Expressing GAL4/VP16 without MYC-EGFP induction permitted low levels of basal MYC-EGFP to bind at both non-E box and E-box promoters.
claims.source: Expressing GAL4/VP16 without MYC-EGFP induction permitted low levels of basal MYC-EGFP to bind at both non-E box and E-box promoters (Figure 7A lanes 9 vs. 10, 13 vs. 14).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Inducing MYC-EGFP while expressing Gal4/VP16 dramatically enhanced the amount of MYC-EGFP bound at promoters.
claims.source: Inducing MYC-EGFP while expressing Gal4/VP16 dramatically enhanced the amount of MYC-EGFP bound at promoters (Figure 7A, lanes 11 vs. 12, 15 vs. 16) especially the E-box-bearing reporter (Figure 7A, lanes 15 vs. 16).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: EZH2 expression was increased by wild-type MYC and mutant-MBIII compared with integrated empty vector.
claims.source: As expected, EZH2 expression was increased by wild-type MYC and mutant-MBIII compared with integrated empty vector, whereas expression was not increased by mutants -MBI, -MBII or -MBIV (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Expression was not increased by mutants -MBI, -MBII or -MBIV.
claims.source: As expected, EZH2 expression was increased by wild-type MYC and mutant-MBIII compared with integrated empty vector, whereas expression was not increased by mutants -MBI, -MBII or -MBIV (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Mutant-MBII MYC bound to EZH2 the same or better than wild-type despite being impaired for transcriptional activity.
claims.source: Mutant-MBII MYC bound to EZH2 the same or better than wild-type despite being impaired for transcriptional activity (Figure 7D); augmented binding with diminished activity upon MBII mutation has been reported previously (Farrell et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7D and a citation to Farrell et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Binding by mutant-MBIII MYC-EGFP not only did not increase but may have been diminished upon induction.
claims.source: Surprisingly, notwithstanding its clear ability to increase promoter output, binding by mutant-MBIII MYC-EGFP not only did not increase but may have been diminished upon induction (Figure 7D), thus inviting consideration that it is productively removed from target genes as part of the transcription-cycle.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The kinetics of MYC binding, action and degradation at promoters are complex in vivo.
claims.source: These data suggest that in vivo, the kinetics of MYC binding, action and degradation at promoters are complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP and expression data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: With increasing MYC, Amax (and Amax/EC50) increase supra-linearly with varying concentrations of competing F4.
claims.source: With increasing MYC, Amax (and Amax/EC50) increase supra-linearly with varying concentrations of competing F4 (Figure 8A and B) or sSMRT (Figure 8D and E) whereas 1/EC50 remains relatively invariant (Figure 8C and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 8A, B, D, and E.

claims.claim: 1/EC50 remains relatively invariant with varying concentrations of F4 or sSMRT.
claims.source: With increasing MYC, Amax (and Amax/EC50) increase supra-linearly with varying concentrations of competing F4 (Figure 8A and B) or sSMRT (Figure 8D and E) whereas 1/EC50 remains relatively invariant (Figure 8C and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 8C and F.

claims.claim: Amax/EC50 is nonzero for zero MYC protein.
claims.source: Also, Amax/EC50 is nonzero for zero MYC protein.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the kinetic analysis data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: MYC is an accelerator acting after the CLS at two (or more) locations and MYC has relatively low binding affinity.
claims.source: The first is that MYC is an accelerator acting after the CLS at two (or more) locations and MYC has relatively low binding affinity.
claims.evidence: This is one of two possible conclusions from the kinetic modeling described in the text and Appendix 1.

claims.claim: MYC is an accelerator or a facilitator of a second accelerator acting at the CLS.
claims.source: The second is that MYC is an accelerator or a facilitator of a second accelerator acting at the CLS.
claims.evidence: This is the second of two possible conclusions from the kinetic modeling described in the text and Appendix 1.

claims.claim: The CLS reaction has consistently been the binding of activated receptor-steroid complex to transfected GREtkLuc reporter.
claims.source: In previous experiments, the CLS reaction has consistently been the binding of activated receptor-steroid complex to transfected GREtkLuc reporter, which is logical as the reporter is the most limited essential accelerator for transcription.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on previous experiments and logical reasoning.

claims.claim: MYC could act as an accelerator after the binding of GR to GRE or be an accelerator/facilitator of GRE through another actor.
claims.source: Thus, MYC could act as an accelerator after the binding of GR to GRE or be an accelerator/facilitator of GRE through another actor (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the kinetic modeling illustrated in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: F4 is acting at two sites, either as a competitive inhibitor of an accelerator before or at the CLS or as an inhibitor of an activator of GRE.
claims.source: This indicates that F4 is acting at two sites, either as a competitive inhibitor of an accelerator (i.e. competitive decelerator) before or at the CLS or as an inhibitor of an activator of GRE.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the quadratic fit of EC50/Amax vs. F4 data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The second option predicts that MYCN is also an activator of GRE.
claims.source: The second option is consistent with F4's action as a known inhibitor of MYC and MYCN (Müller et al., 2014). Thus, the second option predicts that MYCN is also an activator of GRE.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the kinetic modeling and the known action of F4, with citation to Müller et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The results of the MYC-Box mutations that do not alter binding yet change amplification by MYC support the second mode of action, which is that MYC is a facilitator of an accelerator.
claims.source: The results of the MYC-Box mutations that do not alter binding yet change amplification by MYC support the second mode of action, which is that MYC is a facilitator of an accelerator.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MB mutation data in the context of the kinetic model.

claims.claim: This action is also largely independent of MYC's binding affinity to its promoter.
claims.source: This action is also largely independent of MYC's binding affinity to its promoter.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MB mutation data showing uncoupling of binding and activity.

claims.claim: This interpretation predicts that MYC's acts to facilitate the binding of other transcription factors.
claims.source: This interpretation predicts that MYC's acts to facilitate the binding of other transcription factors.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the kinetic modeling and experimental results.

claims.claim: The most straightforward interpretation of these experiments is that MYC is a general amplifier that acts preferentially on highly expressed genes.
claims.source: The most straightforward interpretation of these experiments is that MYC is a general amplifier that acts preferentially on highly expressed genes.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion stated at the end of the Results section.

claims.claim: Ribosomal proteins and rRNA have long been recognized as direct MYC targets from flies to humans.
claims.source: Yet ribosomal proteins and rRNA have long been recognized as direct MYC targets from flies (Grewal et al., 2005) to humans (Gomez-Roman et al., 2003; Grandori et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grewal et al., 2005, Gomez-Roman et al., 2003, and Grandori et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Total RNA is 97% rRNA.
claims.source: Because total RNA is 97% rRNA, the global increase in RNA is primarily due to increased rRNA synthesis.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known fact about RNA composition.

claims.claim: Total RNA and total poly-A RNA generally move in parallel.
claims.source: Since total RNA and total poly-A RNA generally move in parallel, total RNA synthesis is often a reasonable proxy for mRNA synthesis.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a general principle in RNA biology.

claims.claim: U2OS cells contain almost no glucocorticoid receptor (GR).
claims.source: Because U2OS cells contain almost no glucocorticoid receptor (GR) (Blackford et al., 2012; Lee and Simons, 2011; Rogatsky et al., 1997) a small amount of GR was supplied by transfection.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blackford et al., 2012, Lee and Simons, 2011, and Rogatsky et al., 1997.

claims.claim: GRE-activity in U2OS cells is completely dependent on the addition of exogenous glucocorticoids.
claims.source: GRE-activity in these cells has been well-characterized and is completely dependent on the addition of exogenous glucocorticoids (Blackford et al., 2012; Chow et al., 2011; Dougherty et al., 2012; Lee and Simons, 2011; Rogatsky et al., 1997; Tao et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies characterizing GRE activity in U2OS cells.

claims.claim: The MYC-EGFP fusion protein, when expressed homozygously at the Myc locus in mice, dimerizes with Max and supports normal development and physiology.
claims.source: This fusion protein, when expressed homozygously at the Myc locus in mice, dimerizes with Max and supports normal development and physiology (Nie et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nie et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The amount of additional transactivation delivered by added MYC was larger when more GR was used to cause greater activation of the GREtkLuc reporter.
claims.source: Consistent with this theory, the amount of additional transactivation delivered by added MYC was larger when more GR was used to cause greater activation of the GREtkLuc reporter (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: At high concentrations, MYC also weakly amplified the output of GREtkLuc when activated by co-transfected progesterone receptor (PR-B) along with the progestin R5020.
claims.source: At high concentrations, MYC also weakly amplified the output of GREtkLuc when activated by co-transfected progesterone receptor (PR-B) along with the progestin R5020 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The reduced gain of the amplifier with PR relative to GR is explained by the non-linear transfer function.
claims.source: The reduced gain of the amplifier in this case was consistent with weaker activation by PR relative to GR and is explained by the non-linear transfer function (input-output curve according to MYC dose) that has been suggested to be a defining characteristic of MYC amplification (Lorenzin et al., 2016; Nie et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to Lorenzin et al., 2016, Nie et al., 2012, and Wolf et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Mutation of MBIII also enhanced MYC amplification of PR-B.
claims.source: Mutation of MBIII also enhanced MYC amplification of PR-B (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C), and this enhancement was also markedly attenuated by co-mutation of MBI (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C.

claims.claim: MBI mutations have been implicated in the stabilization of MYC protein.
claims.source: While MBI mutations have been implicated in the stabilization of MYC protein, ubiquitylation and turnover of MYC have been associated with increased transactivation .
claims.evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about MBI function.

claims.claim: Ubiquitylation and turnover of MYC have been associated with increased transactivation.
claims.source: While MBI mutations have been implicated in the stabilization of MYC protein, ubiquitylation and turnover of MYC have been associated with increased transactivation .
claims.evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about MYC turnover and activity.

claims.claim: The background RNA seen with the empty vector likely represents random transcription extending throughout the plasmid backbone.
claims.source: The background RNA seen with the empty vector likely represents random transcription extending throughout the plasmid backbone. This is a long recognized problem for quantifying plasmid-encoded mRNAs recovered from transfected cells. (Boshart et al., 1992; Groskreutz and Schenborn, 1997).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to Boshart et al., 1992 and Groskreutz and Schenborn, 1997.

claims.claim: The human genome harbors no orthologous sequences for either the Gal4 DBD or the VP16 activating segment.
claims.source: Importantly the human genome harbors no orthologous sequences for either the Gal4 DBD or the VP16 activating segment.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the human genome.

claims.claim: U2OS cells are unable to drive Gal4 UAS-reporters unless supplied with exogenous GAL4/VP16.
claims.source: Therefore, U2OS cells are unable to drive Gal4 UAS-reporters unless supplied with exogenous GAL4/VP16.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the absence of Gal4 and VP16 orthologs in the human genome.

claims.claim: Alone, Gal4UAS-GAL4/VP16-driven luciferase expression saturated at a low dose (2 ng/well) and then declined slowly.
claims.source: Alone, Gal4UAS-GAL4/VP16-driven luciferase expression saturated at a low dose (2 ng/well) and then declined slowly (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Both luciferase and renilla responses are likely due to squelching.
claims.source: Both responses are likely due to squelching (Gill and Ptashne, 1988), which is when the transcriptional activity of a factor A binding with a target gene is inhibited by another transcription factor B—even when B does not bind to the target.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by a citation to Gill and Ptashne, 1988.

claims.claim: An agent that accelerates a single reaction in a chain of kinetically equivalent steps has limited capacity to increase the output of the end-product yet synergizes effectively with factors that quicken the other steps.
claims.source: An agent that accelerates a single reaction in a chain of kinetically equivalent steps has limited capacity to increase the output of the end-product yet synergizes effectively with factors that quicken the other steps (Chung and Levens, 2005).
claims.evidence: This principle is supported by a citation to Chung and Levens, 2005.

claims.claim: There is no requirement that various accelerators associate physically nor even contemporaneously co-occupy a promoter in the case of transcription.
claims.source: Note that in the case of transcription, there is no requirement that these various accelerators associate physically nor even contemporaneously co-occupy a promoter.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a principle of kinetic synergy in transcription.

claims.claim: MYC interacts with such a broad spectrum of gene regulatory components that it has the potential to modify virtually any step in the transcription cycle.
claims.source: MYC interacts with such a broad spectrum of gene regulatory components that it has the potential to modify virtually any step in the transcription cycle (Agrawal et al., 2010; Kalkat et al., 2018) to minimize kinetic bottlenecks and increase promoter output.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Agrawal et al., 2010 and Kalkat et al., 2018.

claims.claim: No single MB mutation eliminated transactivation by MYC.
claims.source: No single MB mutation eliminated transactivation by MYC but, to different degrees, each individual mutation modified reporter expression.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the MB mutation data from Figure 3.

claims.claim: Reporter expression was refractory to single MB mutations because either the inactivation of the targeted MBs is incomplete or transcription amplification is sustained by the non-targeted MBs and/or other portions of MYC.
claims.source: That reporter expression was refractory to single MB mutations must reflect either that the inactivation of the targeted MBs is incomplete or that transcription amplification is sustained by the non-targeted MBs and/or other portions of MYC.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MB mutation data.

claims.claim: The crippling of amplification by MB double and triple-mutants argues that multiple segments of MYC cooperate to enforce higher output.
claims.source: The crippling of amplification by MB double and triple-mutants argues that multiple segments of MYC cooperate to enforce higher output.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MB mutation data from Figure 3.

claims.claim: Each of the MBs associates with or is in close proximity to a characteristic set of proteins.
claims.source: Much biochemical evidence indicates that each of the MBs associates with or is in close proximity to a characteristic set of proteins.
claims.evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about MB function.

claims.claim: These various protein sets function at different stages of chromatin opening and the transcription cycle.
claims.source: These various protein sets function at different stages of chromatin opening and the transcription cycle.
claims.evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about MB-associated proteins.

claims.claim: The uncoupling of binding and transcription activation by mutant MBs suggests that MYC might act sequentially at several steps, cycling on and off the promoter during a single round of transcription.
claims.source: The uncoupling of binding and transcription activation by mutant MBs suggests that MYC might act sequentially at several steps, cycling on and off the promoter (by dissociation, release or degradation) during a single round of transcription.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the MB mutation data showing uncoupling of binding and activity.

claims.claim: The MBIII mutation that leads to hyperactivity seems also to strip MYC from the EZH2 promoter.
claims.source: The MBIII mutation that leads to hyperactivity seems also to strip MYC from the EZH2 promoter.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the ChIP data in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Co-mutation of MBI blunts MBIII hyperactivation while stabilizing the protein, arguing for MYC-degradation as a step in MYC action.
claims.source: That co-mutation of MBI blunts this hyperactivation while stabilizing the protein argues for MYC-degradation as a step in MYC action, especially in view of MBI's proven role in MYC proteolysis (Farrell and Sears, 2014).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by the data and a citation to Farrell and Sears, 2014.

claims.claim: Degradation or energy-dependent modification of components such as MYC may thermodynamically drive the transcription-cycle forward and improve regulatory precision.
claims.source: Degradation or energy-dependent modification of components such as MYC may thermodynamically drive the transcription-cycle forward and improve regulatory precision (Hopfield, 1974; Hopfield, 1980).
claims.evidence: This principle is supported by citations to Hopfield, 1974 and Hopfield, 1980.

claims.claim: MBII mutation impairs reporter output while increasing both MYC protein levels and EZH2 promoter binding, consistent with activation-driven MYC-degradation.
claims.source: MBII mutation in contrast impairs reporter output while increasing both MYC protein levels and EZH2 promoter binding, again consistent with activation-driven MYC-degradation (Farrell et al., 2013; Farrell and Sears, 2014; Kim et al., 2003; Molinari et al., 1999; Salghetti et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by the data and citations to multiple studies on MYC degradation.

claims.claim: The minimal promoters employed in these studies are devoid of characterized positive-acting cis-elements and are insulated from enhancers.
claims.source: The minimal promoters employed in our studies are devoid of characterized positive-acting cis-elements and are insulated from enhancers, hence they are poorly equipped to recruit and deploy the components that expedite transit of the transcription machinery through the transcription cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Minimal promoters depend upon MYC to supply the complexes that sustain higher expression.
claims.source: Consequently, these promoters depend upon MYC to supply the complexes that sustain higher expression.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of why minimal promoters are useful for studying MYC function.

claims.claim: At high output promoters studded with strong positive cis-elements, multiple transfactors may be recruited that modify and complicate the kinetic landscape upon which MYC acts.
claims.source: In contrast, at high output promoters studded with strong positive cis-elements, multiple transfactors may be recruited that modify and complicate the kinetic landscape upon which MYC acts.
claims.evidence: This is a contrast drawn to explain the advantage of using minimal promoters.

claims.claim: A major advantage of the minimal promoters is that it should greatly reduce the possible sites at which MYC exerts its kinetic activity(s).
claims.source: A major advantage of the minimal promoters, primed by specific transactivators used here, is that it should greatly reduce the possible sites at which MYC exerts its kinetic activity(s).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental design.

claims.claim: The ability to interpret the observed data in terms of a single, internally consistent kinetic mechanistic description is very strong evidence that the model is applicable and the major action of the factor proceeds via that mechanism.
claims.source: The ability to interpret the observed data in terms of a single, internally consistent kinetic mechanistic description is very strong evidence that the model is applicable and the major action of the factor under the experimental conditions being examined proceeds via that mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a principle of kinetic modeling.

claims.claim: Under the conditions of Figure 8, MYC acts predominantly as a facilitator of one or more accelerators acting at or after the CLS.
claims.source: Therefore, while MYC is certainly capable of acting at a variety of sites via different kinetic mechanisms, we can safely conclude that, under the conditions of Figure 8, MYC acts predominantly as a facilitator of one or more accelerators acting at or after the CLS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the kinetic modeling and experimental data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: This interpretation is compatible with both the widely held view that MYC acts late in the transcription-cycle to affect pause-release and with prior and recent reports that MYC acts earlier during transcription initiation.
claims.source: This interpretation is compatible with both the widely held view that MYC acts late in the transcription-cycle to affect pause-release (Baluapuri et al., 2019; Jaenicke et al., 2016; Nie et al., 2012; Rahl et al., 2010) and with prior and recent reports that MYC acts earlier during transcription initiation (Barrett et al., 2005; Tesi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies on MYC function at different stages of transcription.

results.result: Supraphysiological MYC levels are oncogenic and drive pathogenesis in most human malignancies, activating virtually all hallmarks of cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9, and C10 establish the oncogenic role of MYC as foundational knowledge supported by well-established citations (Dang 2012; Hanahan and Weinberg 2011). This represents accepted background information rather than novel findings from this study.

results.result: Two competing models exist for MYC function: the traditional E-box-specific transcription factor model versus the global amplifier model where MYC increases output at all active promoters with gain proportional to promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C11, C12, and C13 describe the two competing hypotheses being tested in this study. These are well-supported by citations and represent the conceptual framework motivating the experimental work.

results.result: Omics studies have failed to resolve MYC's essential role in transcription because statistical parameters, models, and computational algorithms determine their outputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C15 provide critical assessment of prior omics approaches with appropriate citations. This justifies the orthogonal synthetic biology approach taken in this study, though the critique itself could benefit from more specific examples of how parameter choices affect conclusions.

results.result: MYC rapidly increases total cellular RNA, with statistically significant increases at 10 and 14 hours following tamoxifen treatment in MYC-ER cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing time-dependent RNA increases. Claims C73-C75 provide appropriate context about rRNA composition and MYC's known effects on ribosomal genes. The statistical significance is stated but p-values should be more clearly reported in the figure.

results.result: MYC dose-dependently increases reporter output at minimal promoters with or without E-boxes, with non-linear amplification that increases when promoters are activated by GR/DEX.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C18-C21 are supported by experimental data in Figures 1B-C showing linear MYC protein expression with plasmid dose and non-linear reporter amplification. The ~15-fold increase with DEX+MYC (C19) and the interpretation supporting the amplifier model (C20) are well-documented. The non-linearity (C21) is a key observation supporting the amplifier hypothesis.

results.result: Driving minimal promoters with exogenous transcription factors (GR or PR) makes expression more MYC-responsive, with amplifier gain increasing as promoter activation increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C80-C82 demonstrate that MYC amplification scales with promoter activity, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The weaker amplification with PR versus GR (C81-C82) is explained by the non-linear transfer function. This is a key prediction of the amplifier model and is experimentally validated.

results.result: The MYC-MAX dimerization inhibitor 10058-F4 dramatically impairs MYC amplification and abolishes DEX-dependent GREtkLuc activation, indicating that GREtk-promoter activation depends on MYC-MAX dimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by experimental data comparing Figures 1C and 1D. The unexpected finding that F4 abolishes even basal GR activation (C23) is particularly important, though the mechanism requires further investigation. The interpretation (C24) is reasonable but could represent either direct or indirect MYC requirement.

results.result: E-boxes provide only modest (~1.5-fold) enhancement of MYC binding and activity, as predicted from the <100-fold difference in MYC-MAX binding affinity between best and worst 8-mer sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 combine binding affinity data from Guo et al. 2014 (C25) with a calculation (C26) and experimental validation (C27) showing exactly the predicted 1.5-fold enhancement. The quantitative agreement between prediction and experiment (Figure 2B vs C) strongly supports the model that E-boxes modestly boost rather than determine MYC activity.

results.result: At low MYC levels, MAX-MAX dimers prevail and may bind E-boxes more specifically but less avidly than MYC-MAX, with MAX-MAX possessing intrinsic repressor activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by citations to Conacci-Sorrell et al. 2014 and Guo et al. 2014. This provides mechanistic context for why E-box reporters show lower expression at low MYC levels (Figure 2C), though direct experimental validation in this system would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: MYC box mutations differentially affect amplification: MBII mutations attenuate activity, while MBIII and MBIV mutations dramatically boost amplifier gain, with MBIII/IV over-amplification attenuated by co-mutation of MBI.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C30-C33 are supported by systematic mutagenesis data in Figure 3. The differential effects of MB mutations reveal functional specialization, with MBIII appearing to limit over-amplification. The genetic interactions (C33) suggest coordinated regulation among MBs. This is a major mechanistic finding about MYC function.

results.result: MBIII mutations deliver higher reporter output despite reduced protein levels, revealing an inverse relationship between MYC abundance and activity consistent with coupled transactivation and turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C34-C36 are supported by data in Figures 3E, 3I, and 3J showing that hyperactive MBIII mutants have lower protein levels. The inverse correlation (C35) and interpretation linking activity to turnover (C36) are well-supported by multiple citations. This uncoupling of protein level and activity is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: MYC increases reporter RNA levels and mutations do not discriminate between E-box and non-E-box promoters, confirming effects occur at the transcriptional level.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4C showing RNA-level effects. This confirms that amplification is transcriptional rather than post-transcriptional. However, the background RNA issue with empty vector (C86) complicates quantitative interpretation of the data.

results.result: MYC amplifies GAL4/VP16-driven transcription through non-redundant mechanisms, with MBIII mutations dramatically increasing gain and MBI co-mutation reducing MBIII hyperactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by data in Figures 5C-E showing MYC amplification of a completely synthetic transcription system. The synergy (C40) and MB mutation effects parallel those with GR, supporting generality of the amplifier mechanism. This is critical evidence that MYC is a general amplifier rather than having specific synergy with particular factors.

results.result: In chromosomally integrated reporters, MYC and GAL4/VP16 cooperate to drive expression, with E-boxes providing modest enhancement, and amplification resilient to single MB mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by microscopy data in Figure 6B-D showing that the amplifier mechanism operates on integrated chromatin templates. The requirement for both MYC and activator (C45-C46) and modest E-box effect (C47) parallel transfection results. This demonstrates the amplifier model applies to physiologically relevant chromatin contexts.

results.result: MYC-EGFP binding at integrated promoters is enhanced by GAL4/VP16 expression and MYC induction, with E-boxes providing modest enhancement, paralleling the effects on transcriptional output.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 7A showing that MYC binding correlates with transcriptional activation. The dramatic enhancement with both GAL4/VP16 and induced MYC (C54) supports the model that MYC is recruited to active promoters. This provides direct molecular evidence for the amplifier mechanism.

results.result: At the endogenous EZH2 promoter, wild-type MYC and MBIII mutant increase expression, while MBII mutation increases binding but decreases activity, and MBIII mutation may decrease binding despite increasing activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by RT-qPCR and ChIP data in Figures 7B and 7D. The uncoupling of binding and activity for MBII (C57) and especially MBIII (C58) is striking and suggests MYC cycles on and off promoters during transcription. However, the MBIII binding decrease is stated tentatively and would benefit from more replicates.

results.result: Kinetic modeling indicates MYC activates at least two steps in the transcription cycle, acting either as an accelerator after the CLS at multiple locations or as a facilitator of accelerators at the CLS.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C60-C66 are supported by kinetic competition assays in Figure 8A-F and modeling in Appendix 1. The supra-linear increase in Amax with invariant EC50 (C60-C61) supports multi-step activation. The two possible mechanisms (C63-C64) are both consistent with the data. This represents sophisticated kinetic analysis providing mechanistic insight into MYC action.

results.result: F4 acts at two sites as either a competitive decelerator or as an inhibitor of MYC/MYCN activation of GRE, with the second option predicting MYCN also activates GRE.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are based on quadratic fitting of EC50/Amax vs F4 data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). While the two-site interpretation is reasonable, the prediction that MYCN activates GRE (C68) is untested. The kinetic interpretation is sophisticated but would benefit from direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: MB mutations that uncouple binding from activity support MYC acting as a facilitator of accelerators, largely independent of binding affinity, predicting MYC facilitates binding of other transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 integrate MB mutation data with kinetic modeling to propose MYC acts as a facilitator. The uncoupling of binding and activity (especially for MBIII) supports this model. However, the prediction that MYC facilitates other factor binding (C71) requires direct experimental testing.

results.result: The most straightforward interpretation is that MYC is a general amplifier acting preferentially on highly expressed genes.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 represents the main conclusion integrating all experimental results. The evidence from minimal promoters, synthetic activators, E-box effects, chromosomal integration, and kinetic modeling collectively support this interpretation. This is the central finding of the paper.

results.result: MYC transactivation and turnover are coupled, with MBIII mutations causing hyperactivity and reduced promoter binding, MBI mutations stabilizing protein, and degradation potentially driving the transcription cycle forward.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85, C99-C103 integrate protein stability data with activity measurements to propose coupled activation and degradation. The inverse relationship between activity and protein levels (Figure 3J) and the effects of MBI/MBIII co-mutations support this model. Citations to Hopfield provide theoretical framework for energy-dependent proofreading.

results.result: MYC's broad interactions with gene regulatory components enable it to accelerate multiple steps in the transcription cycle through kinetic synergy, with multiple MYC segments cooperating to enforce higher output.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 provide mechanistic framework for understanding MYC amplification through kinetic synergy. The resilience to single MB mutations (C94-C95) but sensitivity to multiple mutations (C96) supports distributed function. This integrates biochemical knowledge with the functional data.

results.result: Each MYC box associates with characteristic protein sets functioning at different stages of chromatin opening and the transcription cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 represent established biochemical knowledge about MB function, providing context for the mutagenesis results. While well-supported by literature, this is background information rather than a novel finding from this study.

results.result: Minimal promoters devoid of positive cis-elements depend on MYC to supply transcription complexes, reducing possible sites of MYC action and simplifying mechanistic interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 justify the experimental design using minimal promoters. This is a strength of the study as it isolates MYC function from confounding genomic influences. The rationale is sound and the approach is appropriate for testing the amplifier hypothesis.

results.result: Under the experimental conditions, MYC acts predominantly as a facilitator of accelerators at or after the CLS, compatible with both pause-release and initiation models.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 represent the kinetic interpretation of the competition assays. The internal consistency of the kinetic model (C108) supports the conclusion that MYC acts as a facilitator (C109). The compatibility with both early and late models (C110) is appropriately cautious, though more direct mechanistic studies would be valuable.

results.result: U2OS cells lack endogenous GR and GRE activity depends on exogenous glucocorticoids, while the MYC-EGFP fusion protein is fully functional.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 establish key properties of the experimental system with appropriate citations. The lack of endogenous GR (C76-C77) ensures clean interpretation of exogenous GR effects. The functionality of MYC-EGFP (C78) validates its use as a proxy for wild-type MYC.

results.result: MBIII mutation enhances MYC amplification of PR-B, with enhancement attenuated by MBI co-mutation.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C showing that MB mutation effects generalize across different nuclear receptors. This strengthens the conclusion that MBIII limits amplification across multiple contexts.

results.result: Background RNA from empty vector likely represents random transcription through the plasmid backbone, a recognized problem for quantifying plasmid-encoded mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 acknowledges a technical limitation in the RT-qPCR experiments with appropriate citations. This is an honest assessment of experimental constraints, though it somewhat limits the quantitative interpretation of RNA-level data in Figure 4C.

results.result: U2OS cells lack Gal4 and VP16 orthologs and cannot drive Gal4 UAS reporters without exogenous GAL4/VP16, which shows saturation and squelching at high doses.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 establish properties of the GAL4/VP16 system. The absence of human orthologs (C87-C88) ensures specificity. The saturation and squelching effects (C89-C90) are expected behaviors that don't compromise the main conclusions about MYC amplification.
